newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Watching, waiting, debating.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Watching, waiting, debating.

text.p: With key economic data not slated until later in the week, the U.S. Treasury market is expected to stick to narrow ranges on Tuesday, amid the debate over what the Federal Reserve will do at its March 25 meeting.
Players said they will wait for February retail sales on Thursday and February producer price and industrial production data on Friday before taking on new and large positions.
"We may be on hold for another few business days," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Due Tuesday are the BTM-Schroders weekly chain store sales report at 0900 EST/1400 GMT, fourth quarter productivity/unit labor costs, January wholesale inventories and the Richmond Fed's February survey an hour later, and the Redbook Research retail sales report for the week ended March 8 at 1455 EST.

"The market is going to be well contained," said Craig Coats, co-head of taxable fixed income at Prudential Securities Inc. "People who wanted to sell have sold and people who looked at the (employment) number on Friday and decided parts of it weren't that bad are putting money back to work."
Some said the dollar could influence the market if it moves significantly.

But the big topic of discussion is the Fed and its Federal Open Market Committee meeting in two weeks. Odds are still seen as below 50 percent that the Fed will raise interest rates in March for the first time in more than two years, although they are greater than they have been for some time.
A Reuters poll of 44 Wall Street economists on Monday showed 17 forecast a rate hike in March, with 34 predicting a tightening by the Fed's subsequent meeting, May 20.
As such, the market is clearly not factoring in a rate hike until May, but the chance of a tightening this month is keeping yields from falling further.

Yields dove on Friday after the February employment report revealed strong job growth with little signs of wage pressures. Market participants now say Treasuries are overbought, although the price declines seen early Monday were wiped out in the afternoon, resulting in Treasuries ending mostly unchanged.
Monday afternoon, the 30-year bond was at 97-17/32, down 1/32 from Friday, while its yield was steady at 6.82 percent.
The two-year note was down 1/32 at 99-19/32 to yield 6.10 percent. These levels are not suggestive of a market anticipating a rate hike very soon, most agreed.
"People don't believe there's enough of a smoking gun" on inflation to trigger the Fed to move, Coats said.

Still, Coats said he is positioned for a rate hike. Should the Fed not move, the two-year note falls to 5.95 percent, he said. "If they do, it'll rise to 6.40-6.50 percent," Coats added. "The risk reward is clearly to be short."

The five-year note was at 99-13/32, down 2/32, to yield 6.39 percent, while the 10-year note was down 1/32 to 97-27/32 to yield 6.56 percent. Bill rates were down two basis points to up two basis points.
